concept.name: Tactical asset allocation
concept.definition: An active portfolio management strategy in which an investor deliberately makes short-term, typically modest adjustments to the long-term strategic asset allocation in response to changing market conditions, valuations, or economic trends.
concept.intuition: You keep your long-term plan but lean a few percent toward or away from an asset class when conditions look unusually favorable or risky, then drift back to the strategic targets.
concept.mechanics: Practitioners monitor indicators such as market trends, valuations, volatility, and interest rates; when predefined criteria are met, they shift a small portion of the portfolio (often 5-10% of assets) for a horizon of months rather than years, and unwind the tilt as conditions normalize.
concept.failure_modes: Tactical shifts require being right frequently enough to overcome transaction costs and taxes; mistimed tilts, especially those driven by emotion rather than rules, can leave the portfolio worse off than simple buy-and-hold rebalancing.
concept.misconceptions: Tactical allocation is not the same as all-or-nothing market timing: it uses predefined signals to make incremental adjustments rather than attempting to call exact market tops and bottoms.
concept.example: An investor whose strategic mix is 60% stocks might cut equities to 52% during a period of sharply elevated volatility, then move back toward 60% as conditions normalize.

citations.source: U.S. Bank, Guide to Tactical Asset Allocation
citations.section: How does tactical asset allocation work?
